claims.text: Laser cladding can deposit a carbide-forming coating that alloys in situ with the substrate.
Laser cladding will create a compositionally or microstructurally graded surface layer.
Rapid laser melting and solidification will produce a fine-grained surface microstructure.
The process will produce evenly distributed carbide precipitates at the surface.
Rapid melting and solidification triggers in situ alloying between the deposited carbide-forming elements and the substrate.
In situ alloying leads to carbide precipitation.
Carbide precipitation mechanically reinforces the surface against wear.
Carbide precipitation chemically reinforces the surface against corrosion.
The carbide-reinforced layer protects the surface against hot-crack initiation.
The laser-clad surface will have greater hardness than both a traditional fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The laser-clad surface will have greater wear resistance than both a traditional fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The laser-clad surface will have greater corrosion resistance than both a traditional fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The laser-clad surface will delay or reduce hot-crack initiation relative to both a traditional fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs produce coarser microstructures than the proposed laser-cladding process.
Traditional fusion-welding repairs provide limited carbide reinforcement.
Untreated damaged surfaces remain susceptible to degradation in aggressive environments.
The intervention is expected to be effective for localized surface repairs when thermal input is controlled.
